query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled single annealing treatment applied immediately after moderate deformation (∼30% cold rolling) in eutectic high-entropy alloys will induce selective recrystallization of the ductile phase while preserving the integrity of the hard phase network, thereby simultaneously increasing both strength and ductility compared to the as‐cast or conventionally annealed state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure comprising a soft face‐centered cubic (FCC) or ductile phase and a hard intermetallic/B2 phase, produced by casting or standard processing.
generation.intervention: Apply a single, optimized short annealing treatment at a temperature just above the recrystallization threshold of the ductile phase, immediately following approximately 30% cold rolling.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under ambient temperature mechanical loading with strain rates typical for structural applications; the alloy must first be deformed moderately to establish differential strain partitioning between the ductile and hard phases.
generation.structural_mediator: A microstructure featuring a fully recrystallized, fine-grained ductile phase embedded within a partially recovered or coarsened hard phase network.
generation.mechanism: The short annealing treatment selectively recrystallizes the strained ductile phase, refining its grain size and enhancing its strain hardening capacity, while the hard phase network remains largely unrecrystallized to maintain strength. This improved strain partitioning minimizes premature plastic instability and promotes simultaneous increases in yield strength and uniform elongation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline as‐cast or conventionally annealed state, the treated alloy should exhibit an approximate 10–20% increase in strength and achieve uniform elongation values around 35% or higher under tensile loading.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEAs in their as‐cast or conventionally annealed state without the intervention of phase-selective recrystallization.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected in eutectic HEAs with a well-defined dual-phase lamellar structure that have undergone moderate deformation (around 30% cold rolling); alloys with significantly different compositions or those subjected to excessive deformation may not respond similarly.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise magnitude of improvement and the optimal annealing duration and temperature window to achieve exclusive recrystallization of the ductile phase without affecting the hard phase.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples with an initial dual-phase lamellar structure. Subject one set to ~30% cold rolling followed by the optimized short annealing treatment at a temperature just above the recrystallization point of the ductile phase. Process a control set with conventional annealing conditions. Perform tensile tests and microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM and EBSD) on both sets.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Uniform elongation or ductility under tensile loading
Grain size distribution and phase fraction of the recrystallized ductile phase
Integrity analysis of the hard phase network
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not yield a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both strength (∼10–20% increase) and ductility (uniform elongation near or exceeding 35%) compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm selective recrystallization of the ductile phase while preserving the hard phase network, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. We have identified the great advantages of PSR on improving the mechanical properties and revealed the unique mechanisms. The main discrepancy between traditional FR EHEAs and the present PSR EHEA is the non-recrystallization state and skeletal morphology of the B2 phase. The key of PSR originates from our critical thinking on tailoring the strain partitioning behaviors in duplex alloys: that is, moderate deformation will induce two different levels of strain in the two phases, where one is for recrystallization while the other can only cause recovery during subsequent thermal treatment. The recovery and recrystallization behaviors of the FCC and B2 phases in the EHEA under different deformation amounts and subsequent annealing were investigated experimentally in Supplementary Fig. 10. Apparently, 30% reduction is a suitable deformation amount to achieve partial recrystallization in FCC while only recovery in B2. Accordingly, the unique processing routes developed for PSR include two cycles of 30% moderate deformation and annealing (Fig. 4a). After one cycle of thermomechanical treatment, the FCC phase in the irregular regions recrystallizes partially (Supplementary Fig. 11a–c). Af

In conclusion, we proposed a universal routine of PSR to ductilize eutectic alloys. The PSR, i.e., individual recrystallization of the soft phase and recovery of the hard phase, was achieved by tailoring the strain partitioning behavior between the two phases of eutectics. Compared with traditional processing methods for eutectic alloys, the PSR prevents premature fracture by eliminating the weak boundaries and thus triggers the intrinsically superior strain hardening capacity of the two phases through dislocation multiplication and potential phase transformation. In a typical FCC/B2 EHEA, ∼35% uniform elongation and ∼2 GPa true stress were achieved. The strain partitioning-dominated PSR mechanism ensures its good adaptability in other duplex alloys, as proven in the A357 alloy. This strategy will open new frontiers of eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials in model civilization by combining their excellent castability and strengthening capacity.

frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) designed for structural applications, which currently exhibit a eutectic microstructure with inherent trade-offs in mechanical performance.
frame.goal: Achieve a simultaneous enhancement in both strength and ductility relative to the current (baseline) performance of these alloys.
frame.limitation: The conventional trade-off where increases in strength typically lead to reduced ductility in eutectic HEAs, making it challenging to optimize both properties with a single modification.
constraints: Intervention must be singular (i.e., one change)
Hypothesis must be testable and falsifiable
Should specify the proposed mechanism, expected improvement relative to a baseline, and conditions under which it is applicable
frame.regime: Testing under conditions representative of structural applications (e.g., ambient temperature mechanical loading and strain rates that mimic service conditions) in a controlled laboratory environment.
prior_attempts: Thermomechanical processing aimed at refining microstructures that improved one property at the expense of the other

decision.trend: Early work focused on designing eutectic HEAs by careful alloying to generate a dual-phase (soft fcc and hard bcc) lamellar microstructure that inherently balanced strength and ductility. Subsequent studies employed thermomechanical processing to refine this lamellar architecture—inheriting, for example, the duplex microstructure—to further enhance mechanical performance. Most recently, targeted processing, such as phase-selective recrystallization, has been used to engineer a microstructure where a recrystallized soft phase is embedded in a hard phase skeleton, thereby achieving simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, the challenge remains to establish a single, controllable intervention that systematically and reproducibly tailors the microstructural architecture (without altering alloy composition) to overcome the traditional strength‐ductility trade-off inherent in eutectic HEAs.
decision.lever: phase-selective recrystallization via an optimized short annealing treatment just above the recrystallization temperature of the ductile phase
decision.why: This intervention follows the trend of using processing to fine-tune microstructure. By applying a controlled thermal treatment that selectively recrystallizes the ductile phase while maintaining the integrity of the hard phase network, the treatment is expected to enhance strain partitioning and trigger in situ strain hardening. This should result in a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility relative to as-cast or conventionally processed eutectic HEAs under structural application conditions.
